interest: 'Dangerous thoughts' in Japan and help for German-Jewish scholars.
overview: This file comprises U.S. State Department diplomatic reporting and internal departmental memoranda from February 1930 to January/February 1934 concerning higher education, student radicalism, and academic affairs in Japan under decimal file 894.4212. The bulk of the collection consists of an extensive February 1930 despatch from Ambassador William R. Castle, Jr. in Tokyo examining the rise of socialist, syndicalist, and Marxist ideologies ('dangerous thoughts') among higher school and university students since World War I, driven by post-war economic distress, disparities in wealth, and bleak employment prospects, alongside the Department of Education's transition from sheer repression toward official ideological guidance. The file also includes a 1932 Embassy report and cross-reference sheet concerning a government ten-year project to reduce admissions to private universities by 30 percent to mitigate educated unemployment, as well as early 1934 Division of Far Eastern Affairs memoranda evaluating an initiative by Japanese scholars such as Dr. Masaharu Anesaki to offer university appointments to displaced German-Jewish academics.

subfiles.about: A comprehensive despatch on the spread of radicalism and Marxism among Japanese students and the Ministry of Education's program of thought control.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador William R. Castle, Jr. traces the rise of student interest in democracy, socialism, and Marxism in Japan from the end of the First World War through the post-war depression, linking it to stark wealth disparities and feared graduate poverty. He observes that student radicalism has shifted from private institutions to government imperial universities, most notably Tokyo Imperial University, which alarms officials because imperial university graduates staff the civil service. The despatch reviews thirteen recent student disturbances and analyzes a new four-point Department of Education plan designed to steer students back to orthodoxy through economic assistance, teacher mentorship outside class, reformed student associations, and state-sponsored lectures on social theories.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 41 from Ambassador Castle on Student Radicalism and Government Thought Guidance
